Unemployment as a share of the civilian labor force, 1929–1933.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series, as published in the Economic Report of the President, Table B-22.

source: original; stimulus table built from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series
stem: The table best supports which of the following claims about the Depression by 1933?

options.text: Joblessness had grown far worse since 1929
Unemployment had returned to its 1929 level
options.misconception: Unemployment in 1933 was 24.9 percent, against 3.2 percent in 1929. It had not returned to its old level.

options.text: Most workers had found jobs in new industries
options.misconception: The table shows the opposite: by 1933 nearly a quarter of workers had no job at all.
The Depression was at its worst in 1933, with unemployment at its peak. It had not ended.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the rate climbed every year after the crash, from 3.2 percent in 1929 to 24.9 percent in 1933, with no recovery yet.
rationales.B: The table shows 24.9 percent in 1933, far above the 3.2 percent of 1929.
rationales.C: Background from the books: factories were closing and laying workers off, not hiring them into new industries.
rationales.D: Background from the books: 1933 was the trough of the Depression, the year unemployment peaked, not the year it ended.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the first and last rows: 3.2 percent in 1929, 24.9 percent in 1933.
2. Ask whether the rise ever turned around: it did not, it climbed every year.
3. Ask what that means for 1933: the worst year, not a recovery.
4. Joblessness had grown far worse since 1929.
Remember: a table's last row is the end of the story so far, so compare it with the first.
